concepts.title: Excess Demand, Excess Supply and Price Adjustment

questions.q: Compute the shortage at a price below the clearing level from the two curves. Use the method 'Excess Demand, Excess Supply and Price Adjustment'. Work with: quantity_demanded = 20, quantity_supplied = 12. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of excess_demand_at_price.
questions.a: 8 rupees

questions.q: Find the surplus of goods at a price higher than the market clearing price. Use the method 'Excess Demand, Excess Supply and Price Adjustment'. Work with: quantity_demanded = 50, quantity_supplied = 20. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of excess_demand_at_price.
questions.a: 30 rupees

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Excess Demand, Excess Supply and Price Adjustment' refers to.
questions.a: At any price below the clearing level buyers want more than sellers offer - excess demand - and price is bid up; above it sellers offer more than buyers take - excess supply - and price is cut, the invisible hand pushing the market back to equilibrium.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Excess Demand, Excess Supply and Price Adjustment'.
questions.a: Shortages raise price, gluts lower it, and the drift stops only where the market clears.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Excess Demand, Excess Supply and Price Adjustment', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: excess_demand_at_price = quantity_demanded - quantity_supplied

concepts.title: Labour Market: Wage Determination and the Demand for Labour

questions.q: Using the method 'Labour Market: Wage Determination and the Demand for Labour', work with: marginal_product_of_labour = 20, marginal_revenue = 8. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of marginal_revenue_product_of_labour.
questions.a: 160 per cent

questions.q: Take the relation taught for 'Labour Market: Wage Determination and the Demand for Labour' and work with: marginal_product_of_labour = 25, marginal_revenue = 15. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of marginal_revenue_product_of_labour.
questions.a: 375 per cent

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Labour Market: Wage Determination and the Demand for Labour' refers to.
questions.a: Firms hire labour until the wage equals the marginal revenue product of labour - the extra revenue from one more worker - which under price taking equals price times marginal product; households weigh income against leisure, giving an upward-sloping market supply of labour, and the wage settles where the two curves cross.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Labour Market: Wage Determination and the Demand for Labour'.
questions.a: Hiring stops where the last worker adds exactly what the wage costs, and that rule slopes labour demand downward.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Labour Market: Wage Determination and the Demand for Labour', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: marginal_revenue_product_of_labour = marginal_revenue * marginal_product_of_labour

concepts.title: Effects of a Demand Shift on Equilibrium

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Effects of a Demand Shift on Equilibrium' refers to.
questions.a: With the number of firms fixed, a rightward shift of demand - from higher incomes for a normal good or more buyers - raises both equilibrium price and quantity, while a leftward shift lowers both; price and quantity always move together when demand shifts.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Effects of a Demand Shift on Equilibrium'.
questions.a: Move demand and equilibrium slides along the supply curve, carrying price and quantity in the same direction.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Effects of a Demand Shift on Equilibrium', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: demand_shift_right implies price_up and quantity_up (supply unchanged)

concepts.title: Effects of a Supply Shift on Equilibrium

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Effects of a Supply Shift on Equilibrium' refers to.
questions.a: With demand unchanged, a leftward supply shift - say from costlier inputs - raises equilibrium price and lowers quantity, while a rightward supply shift from better technology or more firms lowers price and raises quantity; price and quantity move in opposite directions when supply shifts.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Effects of a Supply Shift on Equilibrium'.
questions.a: Move supply and equilibrium slides along the demand curve, pushing price and quantity in opposite directions.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Effects of a Supply Shift on Equilibrium', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: supply_shift_left implies price_up and quantity_down (demand unchanged)

concepts.title: Simultaneous Shifts of Demand and Supply

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Simultaneous Shifts of Demand and Supply' refers to.
questions.a: When both curves move at once, one equilibrium variable is pinned down by the direction of the shifts and the other depends on their relative size: same-direction shifts fix quantity but leave price ambiguous, opposite-direction shifts fix price but leave quantity ambiguous.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Simultaneous Shifts of Demand and Supply'.
questions.a: A shift fixes its own variable - demand governs quantity direction, supply governs price direction - and magnitudes settle the rest.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Simultaneous Shifts of Demand and Supply', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: both_shift_right implies quantity_up; price_ambiguous (depends on magnitudes)

concepts.title: Free Entry and Exit: Price at Minimum Average Cost and Number of Firms

questions.q: Using the method 'Free Entry and Exit: Price at Minimum Average Cost and Number of Firms', work with: demand_intercept = 60, demand_slope = 6, minimum_average_cost = 10, output_per_firm = 40. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of number_of_firms.
questions.a: 0 units

questions.q: Take the relation taught for 'Free Entry and Exit: Price at Minimum Average Cost and Number of Firms' and work with: demand_intercept = 100, demand_slope = 6, minimum_average_cost = 10, output_per_firm = 40. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of number_of_firms.
questions.a: 1 units

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Free Entry and Exit: Price at Minimum Average Cost and Number of Firms' refers to.
questions.a: With identical firms free to enter or leave, supernormal profits attract entrants and losses drive exits until price settles at the minimum average cost; the equilibrium quantity is whatever demand absorbs at that price, and the number of firms is that quantity divided by each firm's output.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Free Entry and Exit: Price at Minimum Average Cost and Number of Firms'.
questions.a: Entry and exit police profits to normal, pinning price at the average cost floor while quantity follows demand.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Free Entry and Exit: Price at Minimum Average Cost and Number of Firms', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: number_of_firms = equilibrium_quantity / output_per_firm

questions.q: Using the method 'Price Ceiling and Rationing', work with: quantity_demanded_at_ceiling = 360, quantity_supplied_at_ceiling = 120. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of shortage_from_ceiling.
questions.a: 240 years

questions.q: Take the relation taught for 'Price Ceiling and Rationing' and work with: quantity_demanded_at_ceiling = 60, quantity_supplied_at_ceiling = 24. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of shortage_from_ceiling.
questions.a: 36 years

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Price Ceiling and Rationing' refers to.
questions.a: A price ceiling is a government-imposed maximum set below the market clearing price for essentials; it creates a shortage that is usually shared out by rationing through fair price shops, bringing long queues and the risk of a black market.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Price Ceiling and Rationing'.
questions.a: Capping the price below equilibrium makes goods cheaper but scarcer, so rationing must ration out the shortfall.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Price Ceiling and Rationing', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: shortage_from_ceiling = quantity_demanded_at_ceiling - quantity_supplied_at_ceiling

questions.q: Using the method 'Price Floor and Support Programmes', work with: quantity_demanded_at_floor = 24, quantity_supplied_at_floor = 360. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of surplus_from_floor.
questions.a: 336 rupees

questions.q: Take the relation taught for 'Price Floor and Support Programmes' and work with: quantity_demanded_at_floor = 40, quantity_supplied_at_floor = 4. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of surplus_from_floor.
questions.a: -36 rupees

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Price Floor and Support Programmes' refers to.
questions.a: A price floor is a government-imposed minimum set above the market clearing price, as in farm support prices or minimum wage laws; it creates a surplus that the government must buy up, or in the labour market, potential unemployment.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Price Floor and Support Programmes'.
questions.a: Propping the price above equilibrium rewards sellers per unit but leaves unsold surplus for the state to absorb.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Price Floor and Support Programmes', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: surplus_from_floor = quantity_supplied_at_floor - quantity_demanded_at_floor
